method: Stated answers come from the party's own words or its leader's, dated to when they said it. Answers marked as not said publicly rest on the cited record, such as votes, signed coalition agreements, ministers' actions or an earlier joint-list platform. A blank means the position is genuinely unclear. Compatible economic priorities are not classified as conflict.

questions.label: Haredi draft: men who leave yeshiva
questions.question: Require service from young Haredi men who have left yeshiva?

rz.text: Smotrich set a condition for any draft law: "Whoever is not studying Torah must enlist."

yashar.text: National service for all, where "the only mechanism for deferring service will be an allocation of up to 3% of each annual cohort for outstanding individuals."

bw.text: "A service framework for all: every young man and woman will serve the state," Haredim included.

res.text: "Every citizen will report to the induction center."

poi.text: Winter: "Every young person of service age will report to the state. No sector is above the law."

likud.text: Likud declined to answer, but its MK Boaz Bismuth's 2025 draft bill aimed to enlist half of the Haredi men not in yeshiva within five years.

questions.note: Shas and UTJ differ on men who have left yeshiva. Universal military-or-civilian service proposals also cover this group; the same answer here does not establish agreement about continuing students.

questions.label: Haredi draft: service exemptions
questions.question: Allow exemptions in a military-or-civilian service framework?

shas.text: The Jerusalem Post's summary of Shas and UTJ: "full-time Torah study is a central religious value that should receive legal protection."

utj.text: The Jerusalem Post's summary of Shas and UTJ: "full-time Torah study is a central religious value that should receive legal protection."

rz.text: Smotrich accepts exemptions for men enrolled full-time in yeshiva, on condition that Haredi leaders endorse that "anyone who is not studying must enlist."

likud.text: Likud declined to answer, but its MK Boaz Bismuth's 2025 draft bill let full-time yeshiva students keep deferring service, with the exemption age left at 26.

noam.text: Avi Maoz said he would back only a noncoercive draft bill that Haredi rabbis approve, and those rabbis back the yeshiva exemption.

questions.note: Yashar specifies up to 3% of each annual national cohort; Blue and White proposes quotas and outstanding-individual exceptions without the same quantified limit. Exempting full-time yeshiva students is a different mechanism from either. A general commitment to service for all does not establish the exemption mechanism.

questions.label: Courts: judicial appointments
questions.question: Repeal the 2025 judicial appointments law?

dem.text: Golan, with Lapid, Gantz and Liberman, in a joint statement: "In the next government we will ensure that the law changing the Judicial Selection Committee is repealed" (translated).

yb.text: Liberman, with Lapid, Gantz and Golan, in a joint statement: "In the next government we will ensure that the law changing the Judicial Selection Committee is repealed" (translated).

bw.text: Gantz, with Lapid, Liberman and Golan, in a joint statement: "In the next government we will ensure that the law changing the Judicial Selection Committee is repealed" (translated).

shas.text: Shas was in the coalition that passed the law 67 to 1 in March 2025, while the opposition boycotted the vote.

utj.text: UTJ was in the coalition that passed the law 67 to 1 in March 2025, while the opposition boycotted the vote.

rz.text: Religious Zionism was in the coalition that passed the law 67 to 1 in March 2025, while the opposition boycotted the vote.

otzma.text: Ben Gvir welcomed the law when it passed in March 2025 and said the government should push ahead with the rest of the overhaul.

res.text: The list wants "a new balanced composition" for the Judicial Selection Committee, which would replace the one the 2025 law set.

jl.text: The list wants an appointment mechanism that "preserves judicial independence," which it says the current one does not.

questions.note: Likud's answer is a March 2025 legislative record, not a new campaign response. The opposition leaders' repeal pledge dates from the day the law passed. Repealing the same law does not establish agreement on its replacement.

questions.label: Courts: legislative override
questions.question: Should the Knesset be able to reenact a law struck down by the Supreme Court?

stances.label: Override only with a special majority (70 MKs or more)

yb.text: Liberman proposed a constitutional court and "an override clause with a majority of 70 MKs" (translated).

shas.text: The Haredi parties were the main backers of an override by a bare Knesset majority in early 2023, though they went quiet on it that spring and have not restated it.

utj.text: UTJ made the override clause a condition for joining the 2022 coalition, and the Haredi parties backed an override by a bare Knesset majority in early 2023.

questions.note: The thresholds are substantive differences: Reservists say more than 72 MKs, Yisrael Beytenu's 2023 proposal said 70. Constitutional codification alone supplies no answer on an override.

questions.label: Courts: reasonableness review
questions.question: Narrow the reasonableness standard while retaining it?

stances.label: Abolish it for cabinet and ministers' decisions

likud.text: Likud voted for the July 2023 law barring courts from reviewing the reasonableness of cabinet and ministers' decisions, passed 64 to 0 with the opposition boycotting.

shas.text: Shas voted for the July 2023 law barring courts from reviewing the reasonableness of cabinet and ministers' decisions, passed 64 to 0 with the opposition boycotting.

utj.text: UTJ voted for the July 2023 law barring courts from reviewing the reasonableness of cabinet and ministers' decisions, passed 64 to 0 with the opposition boycotting.

rz.text: Religious Zionism voted for the July 2023 law barring courts from reviewing the reasonableness of cabinet and ministers' decisions, passed 64 to 0 with the opposition boycotting.

otzma.text: Otzma Yehudit voted for the July 2023 law barring courts from reviewing the reasonableness of cabinet and ministers' decisions, passed 64 to 0 with the opposition boycotting.

noam.text: Noam voted for the July 2023 law barring courts from reviewing the reasonableness of cabinet and ministers' decisions, passed 64 to 0 with the opposition boycotting.

questions.note: Opposing abolition in a 2023 vote does not necessarily answer a proposal to narrow the standard in 2026. The abolition answers rest on the same 2023 vote; none of these parties has restated it in this campaign.

questions.label: Religion and state: civil marriage
questions.question: Allow a civil marriage option inside Israel?

stances.label: Split: coalition deals keep the rabbinate's monopoly; senior MKs vote for civil marriage

noam.text: Noam's platform calls for a stronger Chief Rabbinate, which runs all Jewish marriages in Israel.

bw.text: Blue and White has given no 2026 answer, but Gantz sought civil marriage registration in 2021, saying "many are having their basic right to marry taken away from them."

res.text: The list has given no answer, but Yoaz Hendel said as a minister in 2021: "We must provide an alternative for those unable to marry" (translated).

jl.text: The list's platform calls for the separation of religion and state.

questions.note: Some answers are secondary summaries. An older component-party platform is not a current commitment by its entire joint list.

questions.label: Religion and state: Shabbat transport
questions.question: Allow public transport on Shabbat through local choice?

stances.label: Allow local choice / a limited service

bw.text: Blue and White would run public transport on Shabbat "as part of a reform transferring powers to the local authorities" (translated).

jl.text: The Joint List supports running city and intercity public transport on Shabbat, including mass transit (translated); it wants more than local choice.

likud.text: Likud: "We want to connect Israel on the six working days, while keeping Shabbat" (translated), which Ynet reads as keeping the status quo.

rz.text: Ynet reports that Religious Zionism aligns fully with the 83% of its supporters who oppose any change.

shas.text: "Both parties have historically opposed expanding public transportation and other state-supported activity on Shabbat."

utj.text: "Both parties have historically opposed expanding public transportation and other state-supported activity on Shabbat."

noam.text: Noam's platform: "A public Shabbat, stronger Chief Rabbinate and conservative conversion and kashrut policy."

otzma.text: Otzma Yehudit did not answer Ynet in 2026; its 2022 joint list with Religious Zionism said both parties oppose public transport on Shabbat.

questions.note: Bennett's transport statement is from April 20, 2026, before the B'Yachad joint list. The displayed answer records that leader statement, not an adopted joint-list platform. The Democrats and the Joint List told Ynet in August 2026 that they want service across the country, not only local choice.

questions.label: Religion and state: conversion
questions.question: Recognize conversion beyond the Orthodox religious establishment?

rz.text: Its 2022 joint list pledged to "anchor in law the exclusive status of state conversion under the Rabbinate" (translated), and its coalition deal that December said the same.

noam.text: Noam's platform: "A public Shabbat, stronger Chief Rabbinate and conservative conversion and kashrut policy."

likud.text: Likud signed 2022 coalition deals with Religious Zionism and UTJ to recognize only conversions done under the Orthodox Chief Rabbinate.

otzma.text: Otzma Yehudit has not answered; its 2022 joint list with Religious Zionism pledged to make Rabbinate-run state conversion the only recognized route.

questions.note: Civil marriage support does not imply a view about conversion. Yisrael Beytenu has pushed for municipal Orthodox rabbis to convert, which is neither stance here.
